problems.title: UAV Wing — Abrupt Stall
problems.bottleneck:
You are designing a fixed-wing UAV using a NACA 2412 airfoil. At cruise (Re = 500,000, α = 4°) it achieves CL = 0.8 — acceptable. But at α = 12° it stalls abruptly, making recovery unpredictable and unsafe.

Your constraint: cruise CL must stay above 0.75. Find a geometry modification that smooths the stall without sacrificing cruise performance.
problems.hint: Increasing camber delays separation — try the 6-series NACA family.
interview_questions: Run a baseline polar sweep and tell me: where does the NACA 2412 stall, and what does the CL curve look like near stall?
What does the shape of that stall curve tell you about the separation behaviour? Is it gradual or abrupt?
Which geometry parameter would you change to soften the stall, and what physical effect are you expecting?
Run the airfoil you have in mind and compare its stall behaviour to the baseline. What changed?
Does your modified airfoil still meet the cruise CL requirement? How do you know?

problems.title: Regional Transport — Symmetric Airfoil Penalty
problems.bottleneck:
A regional transport wing section uses a NACA 0015 symmetric airfoil inherited from an older design. At cruise conditions (Re = 1,500,000, α = 4°) it achieves L/D = 62 and CL = 0.42 — both below targets. The aerodynamics team needs L/D > 90 and CL > 0.6 simultaneously to meet range and payload requirements.

Constraint: the solution must work at α = 4° without modification to the cruise angle. Find the airfoil geometry that closes both gaps at once.
problems.hint: Symmetric airfoils generate less lift per unit drag than cambered ones at the same angle.
interview_questions: Run a baseline on the NACA 0015. Which of the two gaps — L/D or CL — is larger relative to the target?
Why do you think a symmetric airfoil underperforms at a fixed angle of attack? What geometry feature is it missing?
What single geometry change would you expect to close both gaps simultaneously, and why?
Run your candidate airfoil. Did both metrics improve as expected, or did one trade off against the other?
How sensitive is the result to small changes in camber? Use Monte Carlo or compare two nearby candidates.

problems.title: Micro-UAV — Low Reynolds Dual Constraint
problems.bottleneck:
A micro-UAV wing operates deep in the low Reynolds number regime (Re = 100,000) where laminar separation bubbles dominate and conventional design intuition breaks down. The current NACA 0012 achieves L/D = 25 and CL = 0.65 at the design point (α = 6°).

The mission requires simultaneously: L/D > 20 to meet endurance targets AND CL > 0.8 to maintain level flight at low speed. These constraints conflict — increasing camber raises CL but drag rises steeply at low Re.

Find the airfoil geometry that satisfies both constraints at Re = 100,000, α = 6°.
problems.hint: At low Reynolds numbers, thin highly-cambered airfoils outperform thick ones — conventional wisdom reverses.
interview_questions: Run the baseline NACA 0012 polar. How does the L/D vs alpha curve differ from what you would expect at Re = 1,000,000?
At Re = 100,000, what happens to the boundary layer that makes thick airfoils less effective?
Your instinct might say more camber helps CL — does adding camber also hurt L/D at this Reynolds number? Test it.
After your first candidate, what surprised you most about the result compared to your prediction?
Run a Monte Carlo on your best candidate. How robust is the performance to small geometry variations at this Reynolds number?

problems.title: Solar UAV — Efficiency-Lift Pareto Problem
problems.bottleneck:
A solar-powered surveillance UAV wing uses NACA 2412 at cruise (Re = 600,000, α = 3°, Mach = 0.09). It achieves L/D = 82 and CL = 0.58 — below both mission targets. The mission demands L/D > 95 (endurance budget) AND CL > 0.75 (weight budget) simultaneously at the same operating point.

The trap: increasing camber raises CL but adds profile drag, capping L/D. Reducing thickness cuts drag and boosts L/D but limits maximum lift. Every single-parameter change helps one metric while hurting the other.

The design space contains multiple candidate airfoils that partially meet the targets — but only certain camber-thickness combinations clear both gaps at once. Find the geometry that lies on the right side of the tradeoff frontier.
problems.hint: Map the L/D vs CL tradeoff across several camber and thickness combinations before narrowing down. The Pareto frontier will show you which candidates dominate.
interview_questions: Run a baseline polar on the NACA 2412. Which of the two targets — L/D or CL — is further from being met at the cruise point?
If you increase camber to fix the CL gap, what do you expect to happen to L/D? Why?
Try a candidate that addresses your primary concern. Did the other metric move in the direction you expected?
You are now navigating a tradeoff. How are you deciding which combinations to test next — what is your search strategy?
Run a Monte Carlo on your best candidate. Does the uncertainty analysis change which geometry you would commit to?
